title: A Loop You Can Run in a Millisecond: A Scheduler on a Test Clock, and Why Its Time Is an Integer

questions.question: A loop is tested by running it for ten seconds and waiting. What does a scheduler on a test clock change?
options: It takes the next event, sets the clock to its time and runs it, so ten seconds of events run without waiting
It makes the loop faster on the robot
It removes the need for tests
questions.explanation: Ten minutes of a 1 kHz loop was 600001 ticks and no waiting.

questions.question: A 100 Hz sensor and a 10 Hz logger run for ten seconds, with the start and end both ticks. How many times does each run?
Why does a tick every 0.1 s up to 0.3 s run 4 times with integer nanoseconds and 3 times with doubles added up?
options: 0.1 is not exact in binary, and three of them make 0.30000000000000004, which is later than 0.3, so the last tick is lost
It is a bug in the loop
questions.explanation: Time is kept as int64 nanoseconds, as in lesson 03-05.

questions.question: The sensor and the logger are both due at 100 ms. The first version of the scheduler ran the logger first. Why?
options: Ties were broken by queue order, and a repeating task queues its next tick as it finishes the last, so the slower task's older event won
questions.explanation: The fix is to break ties by registration order.

questions.question: A task registers another task while the scheduler is calling it. What must the scheduler have done first?
options: Copied the entry's period and task out of the vector, because adding an entry can move the vector and the function being run
questions.explanation: A task at +5 ms ran in the same run, and one at +500 ms waited.

questions.question: Which problem can a scheduler on a test clock not show?
options: A race between two threads, or a task that overruns its period, since tasks take no time and run one at a time
questions.explanation: It models when things happen, not how they overlap.
